title: Foundation of the Original Lubavitch Shul Uncovered
author: Collive.com / Lubavitch Heritage Archive
excerpt: During excavation work adjacent to the Ohel of the Rebbeim, workers uncovered the original foundation of the synagogue that stood beside the graves of the Tzemach Tzedek and Rebbe Maharash — the shul where the Frierdiker Rebbe delivered his final Maamar in Russia.
body:
In December 2018, the restoration team working under Rabbi Gavriel Gordon made a remarkable discovery. Excavations alongside the Ohel of the Tzemach Tzedek and Rebbe Maharash revealed the original foundation of a synagogue — the Akeda Shul — that had bordered the Ohel for generations before being destroyed.

The shul featured red bricks similar in style to 770 Eastern Parkway. Evidence from historical accounts and the physical structure confirmed that this was the same beis medrash where Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn, the sixth Lubavitcher Rebbe, delivered his last Maamar in Russia in 1922, before eventually leaving the country.

Rabbi Gavriel Gordon described the moment of discovery as deeply moving: the last Maamar in Russia was spoken within these walls. Immediately following the discovery, a four-year rebuilding project was launched, ultimately restoring the shul with an Aron Kodesh, Bima, a library of Chabad seforim, and spaces for prayer and study. By 2022, the Akeda Shul was fully functional and receiving visiting groups.
sources: Collive.com (December 11, 2018); Geder Avos project documentation; Rabbi Gavriel Gordon, local Chabad shliach.

title: 500 European Rabbis Return to Lubavitch
author: Chabad.org / Lubavitch Heritage Archive
excerpt: The European Conference of Shluchim brought approximately 500 Chabad rabbis to Lubavitch for a historic pilgrimage — the largest organized group to visit the village in modern times — drawing international attention to the ongoing restoration work.
body:
In August 2016, Lubavitch witnessed an unprecedented gathering. Approximately 500 Chabad rabbis from across Europe traveled together to the village from which their movement takes its name.

The visit, organized as part of the European Conference of Shluchim, brought the rabbis to the Ohel of the Tzemach Tzedek and Rebbe Maharash, where they prayed together, studied, and connected with the physical place that had shaped the movement they represent.

For many, standing in Lubavitch — walking the paths where the Rebbeim had walked, praying at the Ohel — was profoundly emotional. Several described it as completing a circle: from this small Russian village, Chabad had spread to every corner of the world, and now its representatives were returning.

The visit drew significant international media coverage and renewed attention to the importance of completing the restoration work in Lubavitch, including the cemetery, the Chatzer, and the historic buildings of the shtetl.

title: Complete Database of Every Grave in Lubavitch Published
author: Lubavitch Heritage Archive
excerpt: Following years of careful excavation, cleaning, and documentation, a comprehensive database of every grave in the historic Lubavitch cemetery has been compiled — making it possible for descendants and researchers worldwide to find their ancestors.
body:
One of the most significant outcomes of the Geder Avos restoration project led by Rabbi Gavriel Gordon is the creation of a complete database documenting every identified grave in the Lubavitch cemetery.

The project began in earnest after 2018, when hundreds of matzeivos were uncovered from beneath soil and vegetation that had accumulated over decades of neglect. Each stone was photographed, its Hebrew inscription transcribed, and the name, dates, and relationships of the deceased recorded.

The database covers approximately 200 preserved Hebrew-inscribed monuments and is now accessible to researchers, genealogists, and descendants worldwide through the Geder Avos organization. It represents an irreplaceable record of the Jewish community of Lubavitch from the early 19th century through the Holocaust.

Before World War II, the Jewish population of Lubavitch had been over 1,600. On November 4, 1941, 483 Jews were massacred by the Nazi occupiers. The database serves as a memorial to those lost and a bridge to those who survived and built new lives elsewhere.
sources: Geder Avos (gederavos.org); Larimer County Genealogical Society; project documentation.

title: Welcome to the Lubavitch Heritage Project
author: Project Team
excerpt: This archive documents the history, sacred sites, and ongoing restoration work in Lubavitch — the Russian village that gave the Chabad-Lubavitch movement its name and served as its spiritual center for over a century.
body:
Lubavitch — known in Russian as Lyubavichi — is a small village in the Smolensk region of Russia. For 102 years, from 1813 to 1916, it was the home of the Chabad-Lubavitch Rebbeim and the center of a movement that now spans every continent.

The third and fourth Lubavitcher Rebbeim — the Tzemach Tzedek and the Rebbe Maharash — are buried in Lubavitch. The Yeshivah Tomchei Temimim, founded here in 1897, shaped the character of Chabad education worldwide. The Ohel, the cemetery, the Chatzer, and the surrounding streets carry memories that connect millions of people around the world to a single place.

This archive brings together historical documents, restoration updates, photographs, and information about the living work of preservation taking place today under the leadership of Rabbi Gavriel Gordon, the local Chabad emissary, in partnership with Geder Avos.

If you have photographs, documents, maps, or family stories connected to Lubavitch, we invite you to share them. Every image and testimony helps preserve this history for future generations.
sources: Wikipedia; Chabadpedia; Geder Avos; Chabad.org; public historical sources.
